investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What does the Short Synacthen Test assess, and using what agent?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: It assesses adrenal cortex cortisol reserve to diagnose adrenal insufficiency, using 250 µg of synthetic ACTH (tetracosactide/Synacthen) IM or IV, with serum cortisol measured at baseline and 30 (±60) min.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What peak cortisol thresholds exclude primary adrenal insufficiency?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Classically a peak >550 nmol/L (older polyclonal assays); newer monoclonal/LC-MS assays use ~>420–450 nmol/L. Thresholds are assay- and lab-dependent, so always read against the local reference.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: How does paired ACTH separate the two causes of a failed SST?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Failed cortisol rise with HIGH ACTH = primary (Addison's)
  • failed rise with LOW or inappropriately normal ACTH = secondary (pituitary/hypothalamic) insufficiency with adrenal atrophy.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Why can the SST be falsely normal, and what is the gold-standard alternative?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: In recent-onset secondary insufficiency (acute pituitary damage or abrupt steroid withdrawal) the adrenal has not yet atrophied and still responds to exogenous ACTH. The insulin tolerance test, which tests the whole HPA axis, is the gold standard here.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Key safety and interference points for the SST?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Do not delay hydrocortisone in suspected adrenal crisis to perform the test — treat empirically. Hydrocortisone cross-reacts in the cortisol assay (use dexamethasone for cover); oral oestrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin and can falsely elevate total cortisol.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What does a 9am serum cortisol screen for, and why is 9am chosen?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: It screens for adrenal insufficiency. 9am is the diurnal peak of cortisol, so a healthy HPA axis should generate a high value; a low peak suggests insufficiency.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Give the 9am cortisol cut-offs for adrenal insufficiency.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• <100 nmol/L: insufficiency likely, do Short Synacthen Test
  • 100–400 nmol/L: indeterminate, needs dynamic testing
  • >400–500 nmol/L: intact axis, insufficiency unlikely.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Describe the overnight 1mg dexamethasone suppression test protocol and its threshold.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Give 1mg dexamethasone orally at 23:00, measure serum cortisol at 09:00 next morning. Normal: suppression to <50 nmol/L (Cushing's excluded). Failure to suppress >50 nmol/L is a positive screen for cortisol excess.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Why can oestrogens (combined pill, pregnancy, HRT) cause a false-positive dexamethasone suppression test?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Oestrogens raise cortisol-binding globulin (CBG). The assay measures total cortisol, so an inflated CBG raises total cortisol and produces apparent non-suppression despite a normal axis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: In suspected adrenal crisis, how should the 9am cortisol result be used?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Do not wait for it. Take the cortisol (and ACTH) sample but give IV hydrocortisone immediately. In a critically ill patient cortisol should be high, so a normal/low value indicates insufficiency.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What does the LOW-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST) establish, and what is the protocol?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: It confirms whether pathological cortisol excess (Cushing's syndrome) is present after a positive screen. Protocol: 0.5mg dexamethasone every 6h for 48h (or overnight 1mg). Failure of cortisol to suppress below 50 nmol/L confirms Cushing's syndrome.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What is the HIGH-dose dexamethasone suppression test (HDDST) used for, and the key suppression pattern?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: It localises the cause of proven Cushing's. Protocol: 2mg every 6h for 48h. Pituitary Cushing's DISEASE typically suppresses cortisol by at least 50% (partial feedback retained), whereas ectopic ACTH and adrenal tumours do NOT suppress.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: How does plasma ACTH classify the cause of Cushing's syndrome?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Low/suppressed ACTH = ACTH-independent, i.e. an adrenal cause (adenoma or carcinoma)
  • Normal/high ACTH = ACTH-dependent, i.e. pituitary Cushing's disease or ectopic ACTH secretion.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: How are pituitary and ectopic sources of ACTH distinguished when the HDDST is equivocal?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) is the gold standard, showing a central:peripheral ACTH gradient if the source is pituitary. The CRH stimulation test complements it: pituitary adenomas give an exaggerated ACTH/cortisol response, ectopic sources usually do not.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Which factors cause a false 'failure to suppress' on dexamethasone testing?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Pseudo-Cushing's states (chronic alcohol, severe depression, obesity, poorly controlled diabetes) and drug interference from enzyme inducers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin) that accelerate dexamethasone metabolism. Oestrogens/pregnancy raise cortisol-binding globulin and distort total cortisol.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What is the Insulin Tolerance Test (ITT) the gold-standard dynamic test for?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Assessing the integrity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (ACTH/cortisol) axis and the growth hormone (GH) axis simultaneously, by inducing controlled hypoglycaemia as a physiological stressor.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What insulin dose is used and what glucose target must be reached for the ITT to be valid?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Soluble insulin ~0.15 U/kg IV; the test is only valid once blood glucose falls below 2.2 mmol/L with symptoms of hypoglycaemia (sweating, tachycardia).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What cortisol and GH peaks indicate an intact axis on the ITT?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: An adequate response is a peak cortisol of at least 500 nmol/L (assay-dependent) and a peak GH of roughly 5–7 micrograms/L, which exclude ACTH/cortisol and GH deficiency respectively.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Why can the ITT detect secondary adrenal insufficiency that the Short Synacthen Test misses?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: In recent-onset secondary (ACTH-dependent) insufficiency the adrenal glands have not yet atrophied, so they still respond to exogenous Synacthen; the ITT directly tests the pituitary's ability to mount an ACTH/cortisol response to stress and so unmasks the defect.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: List the main contraindications and safety requirements of the ITT.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
Contraindicated in
  • ischaemic heart disease
  • epilepsy/seizures
  • and untreated hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency.
Requires close medical supervision with IV dextrose and hydrocortisone immediately available to treat severe hypoglycaemia.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What are the three first-line screening tests for Cushing's syndrome?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC)
  • late-night (midnight) salivary cortisol
  • and the overnight/low-dose dexamethasone suppression test.
At least two different first-line tests should be abnormal before confirming hypercortisolism.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Why does urinary free cortisol rise disproportionately in Cushing's syndrome?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Normally ~90% of cortisol is protein-bound (to cortisol-binding globulin) and only the free fraction is filtered into urine. In cortisol excess the binding globulin saturates, so the free fraction and hence urinary excretion rise steeply. UFC gives an integrated 24-hour measure of secretion.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What physiological abnormality does late-night salivary cortisol detect?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Loss of the normal circadian nadir. Healthy people reach their cortisol trough around midnight; in Cushing's this fall does not happen, so an elevated late-night (23:00-midnight) salivary cortisol is a sensitive positive screen. Saliva reflects the free, active cortisol fraction.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What UFC level is considered highly suggestive of genuine cortisol excess, and how many collections are advised?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: A UFC greater than 3–4 times the upper limit of normal is highly suggestive. Because excretion is variable, 2–3 separate 24-hour collections are recommended, with a simultaneous urinary creatinine to confirm the collection is complete.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: List common causes of false-positive cortisol screening tests (pseudo-Cushing's and artefacts).
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Shift work/disrupted sleep-wake cycle, acute illness, depression, chronic alcohol excess, severe obesity, poorly controlled diabetes and physiological stress (pseudo-Cushing's)
  • plus swab contamination (steroid, blood, food, licorice) or smoking for salivary samples, and high fluid intake for UFC.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What is the screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism, and what pattern is diagnostic?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: The aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR). Primary hyperaldosteronism shows HIGH plasma aldosterone with LOW/suppressed renin, giving a raised ARR.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Why must hypokalaemia be corrected before measuring the ARR?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Low potassium suppresses aldosterone secretion, which can lower the aldosterone level and mask (false-negative) the diagnosis. Potassium should be replaced to normal before screening.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: How do common antihypertensives interfere with the ARR, and which are the safe switches?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Spironolactone/eplerenone invalidate the test (stop ~4–6 weeks)
  • beta-blockers suppress renin (false positive)
  • ACEi/ARB raise renin (false negative).
Doxazosin and verapamil have least effect and are used during testing.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What is the principle of the saline suppression test and the abnormal result?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: An IV saline load expands volume and normally suppresses aldosterone. In primary hyperaldosteronism aldosterone remains inappropriately HIGH (fails to suppress), confirming autonomous secretion.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: After confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism, how is management decided?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
Adrenal CT then adrenal vein sampling to lateralise:
  • a unilateral adenoma (lateralised) is treated with laparoscopic adrenalectomy
  • while bilateral hyperplasia (no lateralisation) is managed with a lifelong MR antagonist.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Why are metanephrines more sensitive/specific than catecholamines for detecting phaeochromocytoma?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Tumour cells metabolise catecholamines to metanephrines (metadrenaline/normetadrenaline) continuously and intracellularly, independent of episodic secretion. This gives a steady signal in plasma and urine, avoiding the false negatives seen when catecholamines are sampled between paroxysms.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Which is the best rule-out test for phaeochromocytoma, and why?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Plasma free metanephrines. They have the highest sensitivity, so a normal result has an excellent negative predictive value and effectively excludes a catecholamine-secreting tumour.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What degree of metanephrine elevation strongly suggests a true phaeochromocytoma versus a false positive?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Elevation greater than 3–4 times the upper limit of normal strongly suggests a genuine tumour. Mild elevations under 3x ULN are frequently false positives from posture, stress, or interfering drugs and should be rechecked.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: How should plasma sampling be prepared to reduce false-positive metanephrines?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Sample after at least 20–30 minutes of supine rest, using posture-appropriate reference ranges. Avoid caffeine, nicotine, exercise and stress, and review interfering drugs such as tricyclics, SNRIs, levodopa and some antihypertensives.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Before surgery for a confirmed phaeochromocytoma, in what order must blockade be given?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Alpha-blockade FIRST (e.g. phenoxybenzamine), then add beta-blockade only afterwards. Unopposed beta-blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can trigger a hypertensive crisis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: The ITT assesses GH deficiency — what is the diagnostic test for GH excess (acromegaly)?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: IGF-1 as the screen, then an OGTT with GH suppression: in acromegaly GH fails to suppress below ~0.4 µg/L after 75 g glucose (a positive test), followed by pituitary MRI to find the adenoma.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: A short Synacthen test confirms adrenal insufficiency — what is the standing treatment?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Start lifelong glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone), and add fludrocortisone if it is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's). Paired ACTH localises primary (high ACTH) vs secondary (low/normal ACTH); give parenteral hydrocortisone immediately in a suspected adrenal crisis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What glucose load is given in a standard adult OGTT?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: 75g of anhydrous glucose dissolved in ~300mL water, drunk over about 5 minutes, after an 8–14 hour overnight fast.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: State the WHO/NICE OGTT venous plasma glucose thresholds for diabetes.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L OR 2-hour glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Define impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and impaired fasting glucose (IFG) on OGTT.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• IGT = 2-hour glucose 7.8–11.0 mmol/L
  • IFG = fasting glucose 6.1–6.9 mmol/L.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What are the NICE OGTT thresholds for gestational diabetes?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Fasting glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L OR 2-hour glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: How does the OGTT diagnose acromegaly?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Growth hormone is measured with the glucose load. In acromegaly GH fails to suppress below 0.4 µg/L (<1 mIU/L), and may paradoxically rise, because autonomous GH secretion is not switched off by hyperglycaemia.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What is the gold-standard test for suspected insulinoma, and what does it exploit?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: The 72-hour supervised inpatient fast. It exploits the fact that fasting hypoglycaemia normally suppresses insulin, whereas an insulinoma secretes insulin autonomously and fails to suppress.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: State Whipple's triad.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• (1) Symptoms/signs of hypoglycaemia
  • (2) a simultaneously LOW measured plasma glucose
  • and (3) relief of symptoms when glucose is given.
All three are needed to call hypoglycaemia clinically significant.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: At the moment of hypoglycaemia, which paired bloods are taken and why?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Glucose (lab-confirmed)
  • insulin
  • C-peptide
  • proinsulin
  • a sulphonylurea screen
  • and beta-hydroxybutyrate.
Together they confirm hyperinsulinism and distinguish endogenous (insulinoma/sulphonylurea) from exogenous insulin.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: How does C-peptide distinguish the causes of hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Insulinoma = high insulin + HIGH C-peptide (+ high proinsulin, negative drug screen)
  • Exogenous/factitious insulin = high insulin + LOW/suppressed C-peptide
  • Sulphonylurea = high insulin + high C-peptide + POSITIVE drug screen.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Why are ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate) LOW in insulinoma-related hypoglycaemia?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis. In hyperinsulinism, low glucose coexists with inappropriately low ketones, unlike normal fasting where hypoglycaemia would drive ketosis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What three conditions does the water deprivation test differentiate?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Cranial (central) diabetes insipidus (deficient ADH)
  • nephrogenic DI (renal resistance to ADH)
  • and primary polydipsia (excessive water intake).
It is used to work up hypotonic polyuria/polydipsia.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: During the deprivation phase, how do the three causes behave?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Normal person and primary polydipsia concentrate the urine (urine osmolality rises, typically >600–800 mOsm/kg)
  • Both cranial and nephrogenic DI fail to concentrate (urine stays dilute) while plasma osmolality rises.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: After giving desmopressin (DDAVP), how are cranial and nephrogenic DI distinguished?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back:
• Cranial DI CONCENTRATES the urine (urine osmolality rises substantially, e.g. >50% or to >600–800) because the kidney responds to exogenous ADH
  • Nephrogenic DI does NOT respond (urine stays dilute) as the kidneys are resistant to ADH.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: When must the water deprivation test be stopped?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Stop if body weight falls by >3% or if plasma sodium/osmolality rises above normal - these indicate dangerous dehydration. The test requires continuous close supervision to prevent hypernatraemic dehydration and to stop surreptitious drinking.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: What is copeptin and why is it useful here?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Copeptin is the stable C-terminal fragment of the ADH (vasopressin) precursor and acts as a surrogate marker of endogenous ADH secretion. Measured at baseline or after hypertonic saline stimulation, it more reliably discriminates DI subtypes and partial forms than the classic water deprivation test.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.front: Once a 72-hour fast biochemically confirms an insulinoma, what happens next?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.back: Localise the tumour — CT/MRI pancreas and endoscopic ultrasound (selective venous sampling if occult) — then surgical enucleation/resection. Diazoxide controls hypoglycaemia if the tumour is unresectable or while awaiting surgery.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What does the Schilling test determine, and what does it NOT tell you?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: It determines the CAUSE (site of the absorptive defect) of a confirmed vitamin B12 deficiency. It does not tell you whether the patient is deficient in the first place.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Why is an IM loading dose of unlabelled B12 given during the Schilling test?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: To saturate plasma and hepatic B12-binding proteins so that any absorbed radiolabelled oral B12 is not retained but spills into the urine, where its excretion can be measured over 24 hours.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: In the Schilling test, what urinary excretion of the labelled dose is considered normal?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Normal is excretion of at least 10% of the oral labelled dose in 24 hours; a value below 10% (often quoted as <7%) indicates B12 malabsorption.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Stage 2 of the Schilling test (repeat with oral intrinsic factor) normalises excretion. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Correction with intrinsic factor indicates the defect was lack of intrinsic factor, i.e. pernicious anaemia (or gastrectomy).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Excretion stays low after intrinsic factor but corrects after a course of antibiotics. What is the cause?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Small bowel bacterial overgrowth. If it fails to correct even after antibiotics, the cause is terminal ileal disease (Crohn's or ileal resection).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What is the biochemical defect in lactose intolerance?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Deficiency of brush-border lactase, so lactose is not hydrolysed to glucose + galactose. Undigested lactose acts as an osmotic load and is fermented by colonic bacteria, causing bloating, flatulence, cramps and osmotic diarrhoea.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Lactose hydrogen breath test: what result indicates malabsorption?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: A rise in breath hydrogen of ≥ 20 ppm above baseline after an oral lactose load. Undigested lactose reaching the colon is fermented by bacteria, producing hydrogen that is absorbed and excreted in the breath.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Blood lactose tolerance test: what defines a positive (abnormal) result?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: A flat glucose curve — a rise of < 1.1 mmol/L (< 20 mg/dL) over baseline after oral lactose, indicating failure to digest lactose into absorbable glucose. A normal rise (≥ 1.1 mmol/L) excludes lactase deficiency.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Distinguish primary from secondary hypolactasia.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back:
• Primary (adult-onset) hypolactasia is a common, genetically programmed decline in lactase activity (LCT gene)
  • Secondary hypolactasia follows mucosal damage — post-gastroenteritis, coeliac disease, Crohn’s — and is often reversible once the mucosa heals.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Two causes of false results in the lactose hydrogen breath test?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back:
• 1) Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) causes early fermentation and a false-positive rise
  • 2) Non-hydrogen (methanogenic) producers consume H₂, giving a false-negative; measuring methane alongside hydrogen helps.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Why can breath hydrogen be used as a marker of bacterial activity in the gut?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Human cells cannot produce hydrogen. Only gut bacteria ferment carbohydrate to H₂ (and archaea to methane), so any rise in exhaled hydrogen reflects bacterial fermentation of the ingested substrate.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What breath-test pattern suggests small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: An early rise in breath hydrogen of ≥20 ppm above baseline within about 90 minutes — before the substrate (glucose or lactulose) would normally reach the colon — indicating fermentation by bacteria in the small bowel.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What is the biochemical principle of the urea breath test for H. pylori?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: H. pylori produces urease. Swallowed ¹³C- (or ¹⁴C-) labelled urea is split by urease into labelled CO₂, which is absorbed and exhaled. Detecting labelled CO₂ in breath confirms active infection.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What drug preparation is required before a urea breath test, and why?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Stop PPIs for 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth for 4 weeks beforehand. These suppress H. pylori urease activity and bacterial load, causing false-negative results.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Why might a hydrogen breath test be falsely negative in some patients?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Around 15% of people are methane producers (methanogens) rather than hydrogen producers, so hydrogen alone stays flat — methane should also be measured. Recent antibiotics can also suppress flora and give a false negative.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis, and which ion does it measure?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: The sweat chloride test (via pilocarpine iontophoresis). It measures the CHLORIDE concentration in sweat, which is abnormally high in CF.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: Why is sweat abnormally salty in cystic fibrosis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Defective CFTR chloride channels cannot reabsorb chloride (and secondarily sodium) from the sweat duct, so both ions remain in the sweat that reaches the skin surface.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: State the sweat chloride diagnostic cut-offs for CF.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back:
• ≥60 mmol/L = diagnostic/consistent with CF
  • 30–59 mmol/L = intermediate/borderline (repeat + CFTR genetic testing)
  • <30 mmol/L = CF unlikely.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: How is sweat generated and collected for the test?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Pilocarpine iontophoresis (drug driven into the skin by a small current) stimulates localised sweating; sweat is collected on filter paper/gauze or a Macroduct coil, then analysed for chloride. An adequate sweat volume is essential.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What typically prompts a sweat chloride test, and how is a positive result confirmed?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: A positive newborn screen (raised immunoreactive trypsinogen, IRT) or clinical suspicion (recurrent chest infections, steatorrhoea/pancreatic insufficiency, failure to thrive, meconium ileus). It is confirmed with CFTR genetic testing.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: What does faecal elastase-1 measure, and what are the cut-offs?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back:
A pancreas-specific enzyme not degraded in transit, so stool levels reflect pancreatic output (screen for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency).
  • >200 normal
  • 100–200 mild–moderate
  • <100 µg/g severe EPI.
It stays valid during ongoing PERT.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.front: A low faecal elastase confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency — what do you do?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorp.back: Start pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT / Creon) with meals and replace fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); investigate the cause (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic cancer). No need to stop PERT to run the test.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Which two M. tuberculosis-specific antigens are used in IGRA, and why are they advantageous over PPD?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: ESAT-6 and CFP-10. They are absent from the BCG vaccine strain and most environmental mycobacteria, so IGRA is not confounded by prior BCG vaccination.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What does an IGRA actually measure?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) released by sensitised memory T-cells when a blood sample is incubated with TB-specific antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10). QuantiFERON quantifies IFN-gamma; T-SPOT counts responding cells.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Do IGRA or TST distinguish latent from active TB?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: No. Both only confirm TB infection (memory T-cell sensitisation). Distinguishing latent from active TB requires clinical assessment, imaging (CXR) and microbiology (sputum smear, culture, NAAT).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: How is the Mantoux/TST performed and read?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: 0.1 mL PPD injected intradermally into the volar forearm; the transverse diameter of induration (not erythema) is read at 48–72 hours and compared against a threshold.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Give two situations causing a false-negative IGRA or TST.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Immunosuppression/anergy (HIV, corticosteroids, anti-TNF biologics) and overwhelming active TB disease. A negative result never excludes active TB in a symptomatic or immunocompromised patient.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: State Light's criteria and how they classify a pleural effusion.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
The fluid is an EXUDATE if ANY ONE holds:
  • (1) pleural/serum protein ratio > 0.5
  • (2) pleural/serum LDH ratio > 0.6
  • (3) pleural LDH > two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.
If none are met, it is a TRANSUDATE. A paired serum sample must be sent to calculate the ratios.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Give the main transudative and exudative causes of a pleural effusion.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• Transudate (raised hydrostatic / low oncotic pressure): heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia
  • Exudate (raised capillary permeability): parapneumonic infection/empyema, malignancy, TB, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, RA/SLE serositis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What pleural fluid pH value in a parapneumonic effusion mandates chest drainage, and why?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: pH < 7.2 indicates a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema and mandates intercostal chest-drain insertion alongside antibiotics. Low pH reflects active bacterial metabolism; antibiotics alone are insufficient and delaying drainage worsens outcome. The pH sample must be collected anaerobically in a blood-gas syringe.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Which additional pleural fluid tests help identify specific causes?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• Glucose (low in empyema, TB, RA, malignancy)
  • cytology (malignant cells)
  • microbiology with Gram stain, culture, AFB and adenosine deaminase (TB)
  • amylase (pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture)
  • triglycerides (chylothorax)
  • and low pH (complicated infection needing drainage).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: How can diuretic-treated heart failure fool Light's criteria, and what test resolves it?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Diuresis concentrates protein and LDH in transudative fluid, so Light's criteria can wrongly label a heart-failure effusion as an exudate. Calculate the serum-effusion albumin gradient: a gradient > 12 g/L indicates a true transudate.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What is bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and how is it obtained?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: During flexible bronchoscopy the scope is wedged in a subsegmental bronchus; warmed sterile saline is instilled in aliquots and re-aspirated to sample the cells, proteins and microorganisms of the distal airways and alveoli (a 'liquid biopsy' of the alveolar lining fluid).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: In the immunocompromised patient, what infections is BAL used to diagnose and how is the fluid processed?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)
  • fungi (Aspergillus, Cryptococcus)
  • mycobacteria
  • and respiratory viruses.
Fluid is sent for microscopy, culture, PCR and silver/Grocott stain (for PCP cysts).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: How does the BAL differential cell count distinguish sarcoidosis from hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Both cause lymphocytosis. Sarcoidosis gives a RAISED CD4:CD8 ratio (>3.5–4, highly specific); hypersensitivity pneumonitis gives a LOW CD4:CD8 ratio, often with very marked lymphocytosis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Which BAL findings indicate diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and pulmonary alveolar proteinosis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• Alveolar haemorrhage: progressively bloodier sequential aliquots plus haemosiderin-laden macrophages
  • Alveolar proteinosis: milky/opaque effluent containing PAS-positive amorphous material.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What does BAL neutrophilia versus eosinophilia suggest?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• Neutrophilia: infection, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) or ARDS
  • Eosinophilia (≥25%): eosinophilic pneumonia or a drug reaction.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What does the Epworth Sleepiness Scale measure and what is its score range?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: A validated questionnaire scoring the likelihood of dozing in 8 everyday situations, each rated 0–3, giving a total of 0–24. A score >10–11 indicates excessive daytime sleepiness.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Define the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) and give the OSA severity cut-offs.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
AHI = number of apnoeas + hypopnoeas per hour of sleep.
  • 5–14 = mild
  • 15–29 = moderate
  • ≥30 = severe OSA.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: Which physiological channels are recorded in full polysomnography?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• EEG (sleep staging)
  • EOG (eye movements/REM)
  • EMG (muscle tone)
  • ECG
  • airflow
  • respiratory effort (chest & abdominal bands)
  • and pulse oximetry (SpO₂).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: How do effort bands distinguish obstructive from central apnoea?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• In obstructive events, chest/abdominal effort continues despite absent airflow (breathing against a closed airway)
  • in central events, respiratory effort is absent.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What is the oxygen desaturation index (ODI) and when is it especially used?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: The number of SpO₂ desaturations (typically ≥3–4%) per hour of sleep. It is the main metric derived from limited home cardiorespiratory (respiratory polygraphy) studies used first-line for suspected OSA.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: When is the MSLT performed relative to polysomnography, and why?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: The day AFTER an overnight PSG. The PSG excludes another cause of disrupted nocturnal sleep (e.g. OSA) and confirms the patient had adequate prior sleep, so the daytime result is valid.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What two variables are measured at each nap in the MSLT?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back:
• Sleep latency (time to fall asleep)
  • and whether a sleep-onset REM period (SOREMP) occurs.
The patient is offered ~5 nap opportunities at 2-hourly intervals.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What are the diagnostic cut-offs supporting narcolepsy on MSLT?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Mean sleep latency ≤8 minutes (pathological sleepiness) PLUS ≥2 SOREMPs across the naps. A SOREMP on the preceding night's PSG can count as one of the two.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: How does MSLT distinguish narcolepsy from idiopathic hypersomnia?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Both show a short mean sleep latency, but idiopathic hypersomnia has NO SOREMPs (fewer than 2), whereas narcolepsy shows ≥2 SOREMPs.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: What preparation/confounders must be addressed before an MSLT?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Stop REM-suppressing drugs (antidepressants) and stimulants beforehand, ensure adequate sleep, and screen for shift work and sleep deprivation, which cause false-positive short latencies and spurious SOREMPs.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: A pre-biologic IGRA is positive and active TB is excluded — what do you do?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Treat latent TB infection: 3 months isoniazid + rifampicin, or 6 months isoniazid. This should be done before starting anti-TNF/immunosuppression. IGRA cannot itself distinguish latent from active TB — exclude active disease first (symptoms, CXR, sputum).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.front: MSLT confirms narcolepsy — what is the management?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Respirato.back: Modafinil first-line for excessive daytime sleepiness, plus sleep hygiene and scheduled daytime naps. Cataplexy is treated with an SNRI or sodium oxybate. Advise the patient about DVLA notification and driving safety.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What is the purpose of a non-invasive liver screen?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: A panel of blood tests (plus first-line ultrasound) to identify the CAUSE of persistently abnormal LFTs or chronic liver disease, before or instead of biopsy. It screens in parallel for viral, autoimmune, metabolic/genetic and lifestyle causes.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: Which autoantibodies and immunoglobulins point to autoimmune hepatitis vs primary biliary cholangitis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Autoimmune hepatitis: raised IgG, positive ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody (SMA), and/or anti-LKM1
  • PBC: positive anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) with raised IgM and a cholestatic (ALP/GGT) pattern.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: How is haemochromatosis screened for and confirmed on a liver screen?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Screen with iron studies: raised ferritin and transferrin saturation (>45–50%). Confirm with HFE genotyping (C282Y homozygosity). Ferritin alone is unreliable as it is an acute-phase reactant.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: Why must caeruloplasmin be checked in a young patient with liver disease?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: A low caeruloplasmin suggests Wilson's disease, which is treatable but fatal if missed. Confirm with 24-hour urinary copper and slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings. Caeruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant, so a normal value does not exclude Wilson's.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: How does the LFT pattern direct interpretation of a liver screen?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Hepatitic (ALT/AST-predominant) pattern points to viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, NAFLD, Wilson's or haemochromatosis
  • Cholestatic (ALP/GGT-predominant) pattern points to PBC, PSC, drugs or obstruction.
NAFLD is the commonest overall cause and a diagnosis of exclusion.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What does FibroScan (transient elastography) measure, and what does it estimate?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: It measures liver stiffness (in kPa) using the velocity of a mechanical shear wave. Stiffness is a surrogate for hepatic fibrosis, allowing non-invasive staging (METAVIR F0-F4) and reducing the need for liver biopsy.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: Why does a stiffer liver give a higher FibroScan reading?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: A stiffer (more fibrotic) liver conducts the shear wave FASTER. Stiffness is proportional to shear-wave velocity squared, so faster propagation = higher kPa = more fibrosis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What FibroScan liver stiffness value suggests cirrhosis (F4)?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Approximately ≥12–15 kPa (aetiology-dependent) suggests cirrhosis, which mandates variceal surveillance and HCC screening. Values <7 kPa indicate minimal/no fibrosis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: List factors that FALSELY raise FibroScan liver stiffness.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Acute hepatitis (high ALT)
  • hepatic congestion (right heart failure)
  • cholestasis
  • and recent food intake (not fasted).
Obesity, ascites and narrow rib spaces cause unreliable/failed readings rather than true elevation.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What is CAP on FibroScan, and what reliability criteria define a valid stiffness result?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
CAP (Controlled Attenuation Parameter, dB/m) quantifies hepatic steatosis (fat). A reliable stiffness result needs
  • ≥10 valid readings
  • success rate ≥60%
  • and IQR/median ratio ≤0.30.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: Which four parameters are used to calculate the FIB-4 index?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Age
  • AST
  • ALT
  • and platelet count.
FIB-4 = (Age x AST) / (Platelets x square-root of ALT).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: State the standard FIB-4 interpretation bands.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• <1.3 = low risk (advanced fibrosis unlikely, manage in primary care)
  • 1.3–3.25 = indeterminate (proceed to ELF/FibroScan)
  • >3.25 = high risk (advanced fibrosis likely, refer).
In patients >65, use a higher low cut-off of about 2.0.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What three markers make up the ELF (Enhanced Liver Fibrosis) score, and what threshold indicates advanced fibrosis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Hyaluronic acid
  • PIIINP (procollagen III N-terminal peptide)
  • and TIMP-1 (tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1).
ELF ≥10.51 indicates advanced fibrosis (some services use a local threshold around 9.8).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What does NICE recommend for testing advanced fibrosis in people with NAFLD, and what is the overall pathway?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: NICE recommends the ELF test to assess for advanced fibrosis. Pathway: simple calculated score (FIB-4) first, then ELF or FibroScan, with liver biopsy reserved for cases that remain unclear.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What is the NAFLD Fibrosis Score (NFS) and how does it differ from FIB-4?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
NFS is an alternative simple non-invasive score for advanced fibrosis using
  • age
  • BMI
  • hyperglycaemia/diabetes
  • AST/ALT ratio
  • platelets
  • and albumin.
Unlike FIB-4 it incorporates BMI, diabetes status and albumin.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What ascitic fluid neutrophil (polymorphonuclear) count diagnoses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: A neutrophil count of ≥250 cells/mm³ diagnoses SBP, regardless of the culture result. This mandates immediate empirical antibiotics (e.g. IV cefotaxime or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus IV albumin.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: How is the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) calculated and what cut-off indicates portal hypertension?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: SAAG = serum albumin − ascitic albumin (same-day samples). A SAAG ≥11 g/L (high gradient) indicates portal hypertension; a SAAG <11 g/L (low gradient) points to a non-portal cause.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: List three high-SAAG (≥11 g/L, portal-hypertensive) causes of ascites.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Cirrhosis
  • heart failure (with a high ascitic protein)
  • and Budd-Chiari syndrome.
These produce a protein-poor transudate driven by raised portal pressure.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: Why is IV albumin given in SBP, and what fluid analyses should be sent from a diagnostic ascitic tap?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
IV albumin reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome and mortality in SBP. Send:
  • cell count/neutrophil differential
  • microscopy & culture (in blood-culture bottles)
  • protein/albumin (for SAAG)
  • and cytology/amylase as indicated.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: How do you correct the ascitic neutrophil count after a traumatic (bloody) tap?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Subtract 1 neutrophil for every 250 red cells/mm³ present, then apply the ≥250 cells/mm³ threshold for SBP. This avoids falsely diagnosing SBP from blood contamination.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: Grading vs staging on liver biopsy — what does each measure?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Grade = severity of necroinflammatory activity (active inflammation)
  • Stage = degree of fibrosis/scarring (architectural progression toward cirrhosis).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: When is the transjugular route preferred over percutaneous liver biopsy?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: When there is coagulopathy or ascites — bleeding drains into the hepatic vein rather than into the peritoneum. It also allows measurement of the hepatic venous pressure gradient (portal pressure).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What is the main (and potentially fatal) complication of liver biopsy, and what must be checked first?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
Bleeding (haemorrhage).
  • Check FBC and clotting (platelets/INR) beforehand
  • stop anticoagulants
  • correct coagulopathy or use a transjugular/plugged approach
  • and group & save.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What does the NAFLD Activity Score (NAS) sum, and what value supports NASH?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: NAS = steatosis (0–3) + lobular inflammation (0–3) + hepatocyte ballooning (0–2). A score ≥5 supports steatohepatitis (NASH) rather than simple steatosis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What is the key limitation of liver biopsy relating to how little tissue is sampled?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Sampling error — the core represents a tiny fraction of the liver, so patchy disease can be under-staged. Compounded by inter-observer variability between pathologists.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What three techniques are used to examine a renal biopsy core?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• Light microscopy (LM – architecture/pattern)
  • immunofluorescence (IF – antibody/complement deposition pattern)
  • and electron microscopy (EM – ultrastructure and deposit location).
The diagnosis comes from combining all three.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: IF pattern: linear IgG along the GBM — diagnosis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture). Contrast with granular 'lumpy-bumpy' IgG/C3 seen in immune-complex GN (post-strep, lupus, IgA).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: EM findings: (a) foot-process effacement with no deposits, (b) subepithelial humps, (c) subepithelial deposits with spikes — diagnoses?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back:
• (a) Minimal change disease
  • (b) post-streptococcal GN
  • (c) membranous nephropathy.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: What is the main complication of percutaneous renal biopsy and why?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Bleeding (haematuria, perinephric haematoma, AV fistula) because the kidney is highly vascular. Rarely uncontrolled bleeding needs embolisation or nephrectomy.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: Which findings must be corrected BEFORE a renal biopsy?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Uncontrolled hypertension and any coagulopathy/bleeding diathesis (check platelets, PT/APTT; stop anticoagulants/antiplatelets). Small shrunken kidneys and a single kidney are (relative) contraindications.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.front: After treating an episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, what prophylaxis is indicated?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatolog.back: Secondary prophylaxis with an oral quinolone (ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin) after any SBP. Primary prophylaxis is considered when ascitic protein is <15 g/L (low-protein ascites) or in high-risk cirrhotics. Acute SBP itself is treated with IV cefotaxime/pip-tazo + IV albumin.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: Why is serial FVC preferred over arterial blood gases for monitoring GBS and myasthenic crisis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: FVC detects a falling trend in respiratory muscle strength hours before failure. Hypoxia and hypercapnia on ABG are LATE, pre-terminal signs, so waiting for an abnormal gas risks emergency rather than elective intubation.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What FVC threshold signals impending neuromuscular respiratory failure and the need for ICU/intubation?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: FVC below 15 mL/kg (roughly 1–1.5 L) indicates impending respiratory failure; a value below ~20–25 mL/kg is an early warning to increase monitoring and alert ICU/anaesthetics.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: State the 20/30/40 rule for predicting need for ventilation.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: Vital capacity < 20 mL/kg, maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP) < 30 cmH₂O, or maximal expiratory pressure (MEP) < 40 cmH₂O predicts the need for ventilatory support.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: Besides the absolute FVC value, what two factors are equally important in the decision to intubate?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: The rate of fall (trend on serial measurement) and bulbar function — a weak cough, unsafe swallow and pooling secretions raise aspiration risk and warrant escalation regardless of the FVC number.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: How is bedside FVC performed and how often in a deteriorating neuromuscular patient?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• Handheld spirometer
  • upright patient
  • maximal inspiration then forced full expiration
  • best of three attempts
  • indexed to ideal body weight (mL/kg).
Repeat every 4–6 hours (more often if falling) and chart the trend.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What does the DaTscan radiotracer ¹²³I-ioflupane (FP-CIT) bind to, and where?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: It binds the presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) on nigrostriatal nerve terminals in the striatum, so uptake reflects the density of surviving presynaptic dopaminergic terminals.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: Describe the appearance of a NORMAL versus an ABNORMAL DaTscan.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• Normal = symmetric comma/crescent-shaped intense uptake in both striata
  • Abnormal = reduced and/or asymmetric uptake shrinking towards a 'full stop'/period, with the putamen affected earliest.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: Which conditions give a REDUCED (abnormal) DaTscan and which give NORMAL uptake?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• Reduced: Parkinson's disease, MSA, PSP (and dementia with Lewy bodies)
  • Normal: essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, vascular parkinsonism, psychogenic tremor (and Alzheimer's disease).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What is the key limitation of the DaTscan?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: It confirms a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit but cannot distinguish Parkinson's disease from other degenerative parkinsonian syndromes (MSA/PSP), which all show reduced striatal uptake.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What patient preparation is required before a DaTscan?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide (or perchlorate) to protect the thyroid from free radioiodine, and withholding drugs that affect DAT binding (e.g. cocaine, methylphenidate, amfetamines, some SSRIs/bupropion). Levodopa does not need to be stopped.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What is the principle behind the ice-pack test in myasthenia gravis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: Cooling reduces acetylcholinesterase activity, so acetylcholine persists longer in the synaptic cleft, transiently improving neuromuscular transmission and lifting the ptotic eyelid.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What magnitude of eyelid change counts as a positive ice-pack test?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: Improvement (lift) in ptosis of at least 2 mm after applying an ice pack to the ptotic lid for about 2 minutes. It is a simple, safe and specific bedside test for ptosis in MG.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: How does the Tensilon (edrophonium) test work, and why is it now rarely used?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: Edrophonium is a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor given IV that briefly raises ACh at the junction and dramatically improves weakness. It is rarely used because of cholinergic risks (bradycardia, cholinergic crisis); atropine and resuscitation must be ready with cardiac monitoring.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What are the mainstay investigations for diagnosing myasthenia gravis?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• Serology (anti-AChR and anti-MuSK antibodies)
  • and neurophysiology: repetitive nerve stimulation showing a decremental response, and single-fibre EMG showing increased jitter (the most sensitive test).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: Which imaging is mandatory once myasthenia gravis is confirmed, and why?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: CT of the chest, to look for a thymoma or thymic hyperplasia, which is associated with MG and may be resectable.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What does the HINTS acronym stand for and in which clinical setting is it used?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew. Used in acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo, spontaneous nystagmus, nausea, unsteadiness) to distinguish peripheral vestibular neuritis from central posterior-circulation/cerebellar stroke.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: On the head impulse test, which result is reassuring and which is worrying?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• An ABNORMAL (positive) test — a corrective refixation saccade — indicates a peripheral lesion and is reassuring
  • A NORMAL head impulse (no saccade) in a patient with acute vertigo is worrying for a central (stroke) cause.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: How does nystagmus differ between peripheral and central causes in AVS?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• Peripheral: unidirectional, horizontal, fatigable (fast phase stays the same direction)
  • Central: direction-changing (gaze-evoked) or vertical/torsional nystagmus.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What does the mnemonic INFARCT signify?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: The central/stroke pattern: Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test. Any one of these three central signs mandates urgent stroke imaging.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: When is HINTS NOT valid, and what still overrides a reassuring result?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: It is valid only in continuous acute vestibular syndrome WITH spontaneous nystagmus — not for episodic or positional (BPPV) dizziness. Any focal neurology, severe headache, or inability to walk unaided still mandates stroke imaging regardless of the pattern.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: In the Rinne test, what does a NEGATIVE result (bone conduction > air conduction) indicate?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: A conductive hearing loss in that ear. Normally air conduction is louder than bone (Rinne positive); when the middle/outer ear is blocked, bone conduction bypasses it and becomes the better pathway.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: In the Weber test, which way does sound lateralise in (a) conductive and (b) sensorineural loss?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• Conductive loss: lateralises TO the affected (poorer) ear
  • Sensorineural loss: lateralises AWAY from the affected ear, to the better-hearing ear.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: What audiogram feature distinguishes conductive from sensorineural hearing loss?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: An air–bone gap (≥10 dB, with bone thresholds better than air) indicates a conductive component. In sensorineural loss both air and bone thresholds are reduced together with no gap.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: Give the classic audiogram patterns for presbycusis, noise-induced loss and otosclerosis.
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• Presbycusis: symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss
  • Noise-induced: sensorineural 4 kHz notch
  • Otosclerosis: conductive loss, often with a Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction ~2 kHz).

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: Why must unilateral/asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss be investigated?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: To exclude a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) with MRI of the internal acoustic meati. Asymmetry, unilateral tinnitus, or sudden SNHL are red flags requiring ENT referral.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: How does the DaTscan result steer treatment?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back: Reduced/abnormal uptake confirms presynaptic parkinsonism (Parkinson's) → start dopaminergic therapy (levodopa). Normal uptake indicates essential tremor → first-line propranolol (or primidone). The scan cannot separate Parkinson's from MSA/PSP.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.front: A GBS or myasthenic crisis patient has a falling serial FVC — what two parallel actions are needed?
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology.back:
• (1) Airway/ventilatory support — ICU, elective intubation (FVC <15 mL/kg or ~1–1.5 L; don't wait for hypoxia)
  • (2) Treat the crisis with IVIg or plasma exchange.
In myasthenic crisis, withhold pyridostigmine while ventilated and exclude a cholinergic crisis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A 42-year-old woman with fatigue, postural hypotension and a borderline 9 am cortisol undergoes a Short Synacthen Test. Which single value is used to interpret the result?
options: The paired renin concentration
The absolute increment from 0 to 30 min only
The baseline (0 min) cortisol alone
The peak stimulated cortisol
The 24-hour urinary free cortisol
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: The peak stimulated cortisol
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Interpretation of the SST rests on the peak stimulated cortisol reaching the assay-specific threshold. A peak above the cut-off (classically >550 nmol/L) excludes primary adrenal insufficiency regardless of the starting value.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: An SST shows a failed cortisol rise. Paired plasma ACTH is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
options: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)
Recent-onset pituitary ACTH deficiency
Secondary adrenal insufficiency
Cushing's syndrome
Normal adrenal function
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A subnormal cortisol response with a high ACTH localises the defect to the adrenal gland itself, confirming primary adrenal insufficiency. The elevated ACTH reflects loss of cortisol negative feedback on a healthy pituitary.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A man develops pituitary apoplexy and is tested a few days later. His SST is normal despite clinical features suggesting ACTH deficiency. What best explains this?
options: Cortisol-binding globulin was congenitally absent
The cortisol assay was cross-reacting with prednisolone
The tetracosactide dose was too high
The adrenal glands have not yet atrophied and still respond to exogenous ACTH
He has primary rather than secondary insufficiency
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: The adrenal glands have not yet atrophied and still respond to exogenous ACTH
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: In very recent-onset secondary insufficiency the adrenal cortex has not had time to atrophy, so it still responds to injected ACTH and gives a falsely normal SST. The insulin tolerance test, which probes the entire HPA axis, is the gold standard in this setting.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A 34-year-old woman with new central obesity, purple striae and hypertension undergoes an overnight 1mg dexamethasone suppression test. Her 09:00 cortisol the next morning is 210 nmol/L. How should this be interpreted?
options: Failure to suppress, a positive screen requiring confirmatory work-up
Normal suppression, excluding Cushing's syndrome
A result that is uninterpretable without a paired ACTH level
Adrenal insufficiency requiring a Short Synacthen Test
An intact axis making any further testing unnecessary
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Failure to suppress, a positive screen requiring confirmatory work-up
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Normal suppression requires a post-dexamethasone cortisol below 50 nmol/L. A value of 210 nmol/L shows failure to suppress, a positive screen for cortisol excess. She should proceed to confirmatory tests such as the 48h low-dose test, late-night salivary cortisol or 24h urinary free cortisol.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A 52-year-old man reports fatigue, weight loss and postural dizziness. His 9am serum cortisol is 65 nmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange a Short Synacthen Test
Repeat the cortisol at midnight to assess the nadir
Perform an overnight 1mg dexamethasone suppression test
Reassure him that adrenal function is normal
Start lifelong hydrocortisone without further testing
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Arrange a Short Synacthen Test
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A 9am cortisol below 100 nmol/L makes adrenal insufficiency likely and mandates dynamic assessment. The Short Synacthen Test measures the adrenal cortisol response to synthetic ACTH and is the appropriate confirmatory investigation.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A patient taking carbamazepine for epilepsy has an overnight dexamethasone suppression test showing a cortisol of 90 nmol/L, but clinical features of Cushing's are absent. What is the most likely explanation?
options: True ACTH-dependent Cushing's disease
Enzyme induction accelerating dexamethasone metabolism, causing a false positive
Raised cortisol-binding globulin from the anticonvulsant
Laboratory failure to detect dexamethasone in the assay
A cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Enzyme induction accelerating dexamethasone metabolism, causing a false positive
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that speeds hepatic clearance of dexamethasone, so plasma levels are too low to suppress ACTH. This produces apparent non-suppression despite a normal axis, a classic false-positive result.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A patient has a positive screening test for Cushing's syndrome. On the low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (0.5mg 6-hourly for 48h), the 48h serum cortisol is 320 nmol/L. What does this result indicate?
options: Indicates Addison's disease
Localises the cause to an ectopic ACTH source
Localises the cause to the pituitary
Normal HPA axis, Cushing's excluded
Confirms Cushing's syndrome (pathological cortisol excess)
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Confirms Cushing's syndrome (pathological cortisol excess)
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Failure of cortisol to suppress below 50 nmol/L on the low-dose test confirms pathological cortisol excess. A value of 320 nmol/L is clear non-suppression, establishing Cushing's syndrome. The low-dose test confirms the diagnosis but does not localise the cause.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: In a patient with confirmed ACTH-dependent Cushing's, the high-dose dexamethasone test shows cortisol falling by 70% from baseline. Which cause is most likely?
options: Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (Cushing's disease)
Adrenal adenoma
Ectopic ACTH secretion from small-cell lung cancer
Adrenal carcinoma
Exogenous steroid administration
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (Cushing's disease)
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Pituitary corticotroph adenomas retain partial negative-feedback sensitivity, so high-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol by at least 50%. Suppression of 70% therefore points to Cushing's disease. Ectopic ACTH and adrenal tumours characteristically fail to suppress.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A patient with Cushing's syndrome has a suppressed (low) plasma ACTH and fails to suppress cortisol on both low- and high-dose dexamethasone testing. Where is the lesion?
options: Adrenal gland
Pituitary gland
Bronchial carcinoid
Lung (ectopic ACTH)
Hypothalamus
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Adrenal gland
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A low ACTH indicates an ACTH-independent, adrenal source producing cortisol autonomously. Autonomous adrenal cortisol suppresses the pituitary ACTH and does not respond to dexamethasone feedback at any dose. This pattern localises the lesion to the adrenal gland.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: During an insulin tolerance test, what biochemical endpoint must be achieved for the test to be considered a valid stimulus?
options: A fall in blood glucose of at least 1 mmol/L from baseline
Blood glucose below 4.0 mmol/L
A doubling of the serum insulin level
A serum cortisol above 500 nmol/L
Blood glucose below 2.2 mmol/L with symptoms of hypoglycaemia
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Blood glucose below 2.2 mmol/L with symptoms of hypoglycaemia
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Adequate hypoglycaemia is the whole point of the test: only a glucose below 2.2 mmol/L accompanied by symptoms provides a strong enough stress to validly probe the GH and ACTH axes. Without this endpoint the results are uninterpretable and the test must be repeated with a higher insulin dose.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A patient develops suspected secondary adrenal insufficiency two weeks after pituitary surgery. Which test most reliably confirms this recent-onset deficiency?
options: Random morning cortisol alone
Short Synacthen (250 microgram ACTH) test
Overnight dexamethasone suppression test
24-hour urinary free cortisol
Insulin tolerance test
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Insulin tolerance test
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: In recent-onset secondary adrenal insufficiency the adrenal glands have not yet atrophied and still respond to exogenous ACTH, so the Short Synacthen Test can be falsely normal. The ITT stresses the whole hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis directly and reliably detects this early defect.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to performing an insulin tolerance test?
options: Well-controlled type 2 diabetes
Ischaemic heart disease
Age over 50 years
A raised prolactin level
Mild iron-deficiency anaemia
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Ischaemic heart disease
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Induced hypoglycaemia triggers a surge of catecholamines that can precipitate arrhythmia or myocardial ischaemia, so ischaemic heart disease is a contraindication and a baseline ECG is required. Epilepsy and untreated hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency are the other key contraindications.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A 44-year-old woman is being screened for Cushing's syndrome with a late-night salivary cortisol test. What is the physiological basis for taking the sample close to midnight?
options: Salivary flow is highest at night, diluting interfering substances
Dexamethasone maximally suppresses the axis at midnight
In Cushing's syndrome the normal midnight cortisol nadir is lost, so a raised value is a sensitive marker
Cortisol-binding globulin concentration peaks at midnight
Renal cortisol clearance is greatest overnight
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: In Cushing's syndrome the normal midnight cortisol nadir is lost, so a raised value is a sensitive marker
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Healthy individuals reach their cortisol trough around midnight due to the circadian rhythm. In Cushing's syndrome this nadir is abolished, so an elevated late-night salivary cortisol is a sensitive screen. Saliva reflects the free, biologically active cortisol fraction.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A patient's 24-hour urinary free cortisol comes back at the lower end of normal, but clinical suspicion of Cushing's is high. Which technical factor most commonly produces a falsely LOW UFC result?
options: Incomplete urine collection with missed voids
Concurrent shift work disrupting the sleep-wake cycle
Sampling performed during an acute illness
Very high fluid intake during the collection
Contamination of the sample with topical steroid
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Incomplete urine collection with missed voids
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A falsely low UFC most often results from an incomplete collection where voids are missed. A simultaneous urinary creatinine helps confirm adequacy, and 2–3 collections are advised because excretion is variable.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: First-line screening returns a single mildly elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol in a man with depression and a high alcohol intake. What is the most appropriate next step before diagnosing Cushing's syndrome?
options: Measure cortisol-binding globulin to confirm the diagnosis
Start medical therapy to lower cortisol immediately
Confirm with at least one further first-line test, recognising possible pseudo-Cushing's
Diagnose Cushing's syndrome and proceed to pituitary imaging
Reassure the patient that Cushing's is excluded
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Confirm with at least one further first-line test, recognising possible pseudo-Cushing's
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A single mildly abnormal test is non-specific, and depression and alcohol excess cause pseudo-Cushing's with mildly raised cortisol. At least two different first-line tests should be abnormal before confirming hypercortisolism, so corroboration with a further test is needed.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A 46-year-old with resistant hypertension and a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L is being screened for Conn's syndrome. Which biochemical pattern best supports primary hyperaldosteronism?
options: Normal aldosterone with high renin
Low aldosterone with high renin
High aldosterone with high renin
Low aldosterone with low renin
High aldosterone with suppressed renin
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: High aldosterone with suppressed renin
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Autonomous adrenal aldosterone secretion causes volume expansion that suppresses renin, producing high aldosterone with low renin and thus a raised ARR. High aldosterone with high renin instead indicates secondary hyperaldosteronism.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: Which medication must be stopped approximately 4–6 weeks before measuring the aldosterone:renin ratio because it directly invalidates the result?
options: Hydralazine
Spironolactone
Doxazosin
Amlodipine
Verapamil
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Spironolactone
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that blocks aldosterone action and markedly distorts renin and aldosterone, so it is withheld for about 4–6 weeks before ARR. Doxazosin and verapamil have minimal effect and are the preferred agents during testing.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A patient with a positive ARR undergoes a saline suppression test. Which result confirms primary hyperaldosteronism?
options: Aldosterone remains inappropriately high after the saline infusion
Aldosterone falls to a low level after the saline infusion
Cortisol fails to suppress after the saline infusion
Renin rises sharply after the saline infusion
Potassium rises after the saline infusion
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Aldosterone remains inappropriately high after the saline infusion
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A saline load expands volume and normally suppresses aldosterone; failure to suppress demonstrates autonomous secretion and confirms primary hyperaldosteronism. Appropriate suppression of aldosterone instead excludes the diagnosis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A 42-year-old with paroxysmal hypertension, episodic headaches, sweating and palpitations is being screened for a catecholamine-secreting tumour. Why are plasma or urinary metanephrines preferred over measuring catecholamines directly?
options: Metanephrines are secreted only during a hypertensive paroxysm
Catecholamines are elevated only in paragangliomas, not phaeochromocytomas
Tumour cells metabolise catecholamines to metanephrines continuously, giving a steady signal despite episodic secretion
Metanephrines are unaffected by any drugs or patient posture
Catecholamines cannot be measured in plasma with current assays
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Tumour cells metabolise catecholamines to metanephrines continuously, giving a steady signal despite episodic secretion
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Phaeochromocytoma cells O-methylate catecholamines to metanephrines intracellularly and continuously, independent of secretory bursts. This constant leak into plasma and urine gives higher sensitivity than catecholamines, which are frequently normal between paroxysms.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A patient's plasma free normetanephrine returns at 1.5 times the upper limit of normal. The sample was taken seated during an acute admission while the patient was on a tricyclic antidepressant. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Proceed directly to MIBG scanning without repeating biochemistry
The result excludes phaeochromocytoma completely
The tricyclic makes the result falsely low
This is a likely false positive; recheck supine after removing interfering factors
This confirms phaeochromocytoma and warrants immediate adrenalectomy
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: This is a likely false positive; recheck supine after removing interfering factors
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A mild elevation under 3x the upper limit, taken seated during acute stress and on a tricyclic, is a classic false-positive pattern. The correct step is to repeat sampling supine after withdrawing interfering drugs and controlling stress. A truly elevated tumour value typically exceeds 3–4x the upper limit.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A phaeochromocytoma is biochemically and radiologically confirmed and surgery is planned. Which pharmacological strategy is correct before the procedure?
options: Use a calcium-channel blocker instead of any adrenergic blockade
Establish alpha-blockade first (e.g. phenoxybenzamine), then add beta-blockade
Give a beta-blocker alone throughout the perioperative period
Start a beta-blocker first, then add an alpha-blocker
Avoid all blockade and rely on intraoperative fluids only
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Establish alpha-blockade first (e.g. phenoxybenzamine), then add beta-blockade
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Alpha-blockade must be established first to control vasoconstriction, with beta-blockade added only afterwards. Giving a beta-blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: A 52-year-old asymptomatic man has an OGTT. Fasting plasma glucose is 6.5 mmol/L and 2-hour glucose is 9.0 mmol/L. How is this best classified?
options: Gestational diabetes
Normal glucose tolerance
Diabetes mellitus
Acromegaly
Impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: Impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: A fasting value of 6.1–6.9 mmol/L defines impaired fasting glucose, and a 2-hour value of 7.8–11.0 mmol/L defines impaired glucose tolerance. Neither value reaches the diabetes thresholds of fasting ≥7.0 or 2-hour ≥11.1 mmol/L.

investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.question: During which part of an OGTT is growth hormone measured, and what result confirms acromegaly?
options: GH rises above 10 µg/L when fasting
GH fails to suppress below 0.4 µg/L after the glucose load
GH is undetectable at 2 hours
GH doubles after an insulin injection
GH suppresses below 0.4 µg/L after the glucose load
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.answer: GH fails to suppress below 0.4 µg/L after the glucose load
investigations__SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine.explanation: Glucose normally suppresses growth hormone secretion. In acromegaly the autonomous GH secretion fails to suppress below 0.4 µg/L (<1 mIU/L) after the oral glucose load, and may even rise paradoxically.
